contract: Ticket 19 criterion 6: closed schemas reject unexpected free text and Program identifiers before handler execution; roster.py:205-210 states it as an absolute, including inside an otherwise opaque payload

DEPTH is raised from 8 to 16 for the same reason the behaviour changed: a bound that refuses has to sit clear of anything a hunter would file, and the deepest contract on this surface is two levels. contract: spec.md:484: Agent responses have target credentials removed, and when removal changes bytes both agent-view and wire-view hashes record the transformation; story 120: agent-visible Artifacts redacted and content-addressed, so that exact bytes can be cited without exposing injected secrets
evidence: project_identity_response returned ([], b"") for every exchange an Identity was bound to, so the Agent view of an authenticated response was the status line and nothing else. That is suppression rather than the redaction the stories describe: nothing was citable, and an access control finding -- the class authenticated hunting exists to produce -- is made of exactly the response body a hunter could no longer read. The rationale in the docstring, that reflection is not safely recognisable, argues for redacting the credential and dropping the fields that carry it, not for withholding the message.
remediation: project_identity_response now takes the values this exchange would spend and removes them. identity.Session.secrets(url) lists them value by value -- each static origin header value, the token half of a scheme-prefixed one, and each cookie crumb from the jar, which by then holds what this response set -- and proxy._renderings spells each one the ways a web application round-trips a value: raw, percent-encoded, base64 standard and urlsafe with and without padding, and hex in both cases. A response header whose name or value carries any of those spellings is dropped whole rather than marked, because a Location reading /continue/[redacted] canonicalises into a URL no target pointed at and the Receipt would record it as this exchange link. A body has each spelling replaced by [redacted], so the Agent reads the answer its own request earned. What is not recoverable by search -- a hash, a truncation, a value split across a template -- stays uncovered by this and covered by the sealed wire view, whose separate hash is what records the transformation.

contract: src/redkraken/store.py:169 -- discard is safe for a ciphertext and false of plaintext, where another Program may already have committed a reference to exactly those bytes
evidence: Four rollback paths in Handler._forward called store.discard(request_sha) and store.discard(response_sha) on the agent-view transcripts, guarded by the flag store.put returns. That flag says this process wrote the file; it does not say nobody has referenced it since. The store is content-addressed and global, so between the put and the refusal another Program can put the same plaintext, be told it was already filed, and commit a reference that this rollback then empties.
remediation: The two puts drop the newness flag and the four plaintext discards are gone; a refused exchange now discards only the envelopes it sealed. Plaintext nobody ends up referencing is retention's to collect: artifacts_due_for_purge is the view that refcounts it across Programs, and no command runs one yet, which is a bounded cost where deleting bytes out from under a committed reference is evidence loss. tests.test_proxy.RollbackTest reads the property off the source so a new rollback arm cannot reintroduce it.

contract: ticket 06 comment -- artifacts_due_for_purge already refcounts across programs; story 45 on retention
evidence: No Python module reads artifacts_due_for_purge: the view is maintained across three migrations and consumed by nothing, so no retention command exists to run it. Separately, sealed_wire_artifacts.ciphertext_sha256 is in no arm and has no artifacts row at all, so the envelope's bytes are outside the refcount the view performs.
remediation: Dispositioned rather than fixed, and named here because the proxy's rollback path now leaves unreferenced plaintext for retention to collect. Implementing the purge is a retention ticket: it needs the command, an artifacts row for each envelope, and a decision about what a Program's purge_after means for bytes another live Program references. Until then the cost is bytes left in the store, which is bounded, against deleting bytes out from under a committed reference, which is evidence loss.

contract: docs/performance-budgets.md: the slate is allowed 1500 ms, and the budget exists to catch an operation that took a tenth of a second starting to take thirty because a join lost its index or a bounded read stopped being bounded
evidence: The case failed at 2626.3 ms, having reported 1140.9 and 1759.6 on earlier runs, against 185 ms measured alone -- tests/test_database.py shares one database across the module and the benchmark runs late, so it measures its own corpus inside tables carrying the whole suite's rows. The scoping is intact: EXPLAIN ANALYZE at 100200 Tasks reports Index Scan using tasks_program_id_label_key with rows=200 and a Nested Loop finishing at actual time=6.664..6.664. What the same plan reports beside it is JIT: Functions: 71, Optimization 228.977 ms, Emission 180.574 ms, Total 430.504 ms against an Execution Time of 437.602 ms. Postgres decides to compile from a cost estimate over the whole relation, so the compilation arrives with rows this Program does not own, is paid per call, and is paid whether or not a Task is offered.
remediation: A migration puts SET jit = off on offer_slate(). The A/B is on the 100200-Task corpus, median of five: 477.6 ms as the schema shipped, 10.0 ms with the clause, 9.9 ms with jit off for the whole session, so on that corpus the compilation was the whole cost. It is not the whole of the case's number and is not recorded as though it were: the benchmark's own corpus costs 186.2 ms alone after the fix, unchanged, because a database that small never crosses jit_above_cost, and the composed run reports 1159.8 ms against the 1500 ms budget. What is fixed here is a per-call tax that grows with an installation and would have reached an operator; what is left is the shared-database condition the case is measured in, which is the case's own and is dispositioned as stub-target-rebuilt-per-proxy-case is. On the function and not the database, because a query that really does grind rows should still be compiled; on offer_slate and not rank_candidates, because the latter is LANGUAGE sql where a SET clause would block inlining and change the plan, and a SET on a PL/pgSQL function covers everything the call executes. The case reads proconfig rather than a clock, so a later CREATE OR REPLACE that drops the clause fails by name instead of by a slow reading.

contract: CONTEXT.md, the Slate entry: the bounded set of tasks the runtime offers the orchestrator to choose from -- Avoid: Queue, candidates, shortlist, options
evidence: The module that offers the Slate, walks it, records the choice over it and claims off it called it a queue in five places of its own narrative: the module docstring, the note on an empty offer, a section rule, a failure message and the capsule docstring. A second name for the Slate is a second thing for an operator, an ADR and a ledger row to be talking about, and this is the module where all three meet.
